newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf Canada in Montana Indian lands deal.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada in Montana Indian lands deal.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd said on Tuesday it signed an agreement with the Assiniboine and Sioux native Indian Tribes of Fort Peck, Montana, giving the company access to exploratory lands.
Gulf said the deal would initially provide it with access to 800,000 acres of tribal and non-tribal land in the 2.1-million-acre Fort Peck Reservation on the western slope of the Williston Basin.
The agreement also gave Gulf an option to expand its program to cover the rest of the reservation, it said.

"This innovative agreement augments Gulf's dynamic land acquisition program and sets us up for further exposure to multi-zone drilling that includes Lodgepole, Red River and other targets," Gulf vice-president Bill Picquet said in a statement.

Under the agreement, the tribes would contribute 110,000 acres of tribal land and Gulf, which is in the process of expanding its exploration acreage in the United States, would contribute the 60,000 acres it currently has leased.
The company is also expected to provide the capital to buy more non-tribal lands to bring the total area covered by the agreement to 800,000 acres.
The agreement, still subject to approval by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior, calls for at least 80 square miles of 3D seismic and four exploratory wells to be drilled within five years.

Gulf said it planned to begin a 60-square-mile seismic program in the first quarter of 1997 and drill up to two wells before the end of next year. Its minimum initial investment was expected to be about US$6.5 million.

Also under the deal, the tribes were to participate in exploration planning and operations and receive 20 percent of net revenue from all production to come from both tribal and non-tribal lands, Gulf said.
The agreement also provided for education and training for the tribes' members, as well as employment opportunities and increased tribal participation in the future.

"Gulf gains access to large tracts of virtually unexplored and highly prospective lands in the Fort Peck region, and we are able to further our objective of increased tribal ownership of resources, essentially at no risk," Tribal chairman Caleb Shields said. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
